facts.title: AReaL-DTE: Sparse Policy-Weight Transfer for Online Agentic Reinforcement Learning
facts.event_hint: AReaL-DTE: a snapshot-free Delta Transfer Engine for online agentic RL that exploits inference-visible weight sparsity (<2% of BF16 elements change between consecutive policy versions) to make frequent policy-weight synchronization between training and rollout workers sparse across the full data path (construction, layout translation, transfer, application).
facts.problem: Online agentic RL with micro-services separates policy training from rollout generation, making frequent policy-weight synchronization a critical systems overhead. Shared storage connects these services across clusters, but vanilla dense synchronization incurs model-scale construction/transfer/application cost. Existing sparse/checkpoint-oriented approaches (e.g., PULSE) still retain a previous-model checkpoint and materialize complete intermediates to bridge heterogeneous training (Megatron-LM/FSDP) and inference (vLLM/SGLang) layouts (different parameter names, fusion/permutation rules, dtypes, TP/PP/DP/EP layouts). For a policy with N inference-visible elements, a dense refresh constructs, stages, transfers, and applies O(N) values even when the new policy differs at only a small fraction of positions.
facts.mechanism: AReaL-DTE is a snapshot-free Delta Transfer Engine that translates inference-visible weight sparsity into end-to-end efficiency. (1) On-demand reconstruction of overwritten weights by inverting AdamW updates (streaming AdamW inversion), avoiding a persistent historical snapshot. (2) Streams reconstructed and current parameters through converter-aligned BF16 change detection (after aligned conversion to the receiver's layout). (3) Remaps changed elements directly into receiver-local coordinates and delivers receiver-specific updates. Two transports: manifest-committed sparse transfer through shared storage (OSS) across clusters, and a deadlock-safe two-round protocol within a cluster followed by direct scatter-application to inference shards. Preserves layout translation while avoiding a complete-model representation for each refresh; relies on the surrounding control/storage layer for version ordering and consistency. Does not change the rollout schedule, RL algorithm, or consistency policy.

evidence.claim: Cross-cluster E2E synchronization latency (Table 2a, Qwen3-30B-A3B, derived as T_same,disk + T_upload,p50 + T_download,p50 over Alibaba OSS, Zstd-compressed, bandwidth 0.1/1/10 Gbps): AReaL-DTE 477.47/71.31/30.70 s on GSM8K vs ByteCheckpoint 8741.18/1080.12/314.05 s and PULSE 544.86/140.90/99.43 s. Speedups up to 19.9x over ByteCheckpoint and 3.2x over PULSE (the PULSE gap widens with bandwidth, reaching 3.2x at 10 Gbps).
evidence.value: Qwen3-30B-A3B GSM8K: 477.47/71.31/30.70 s (0.1/1/10 Gbps); up to 19.9x vs ByteCheckpoint, 3.2x vs PULSE
evidence.baseline: ByteCheckpoint (dense complete-state checkpoint); PULSE (sparse changed-values but retains previous checkpoint)
evidence.condition: Qwen3-30B-A3B, 16 H200 GPUs, storage-mediated cross-cluster, Alibaba OSS, Zstd, 0.1/1/10 Gbps
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 11 (Table 2a); PDF Page 12 (Section 5.3 narrative)

evidence.claim: Same-cluster E2E synchronization latency (Table 3, Qwen3-8B): AReaL-DTE synchronizes Qwen3-8B in 2.77-2.87 s, yielding speedups up to 7.6x over ByteCheckpoint-NCCL and 7.4x over PULSE-NCCL; benefit comes from constructing receiver-specific sparse updates and applying them directly to destination shards. (Abstract reports up to 7.6x and 7.4x within a cluster.)
evidence.value: Qwen3-8B same-cluster 2.77-2.87 s; up to 7.6x vs ByteCheckpoint-NCCL, 7.4x vs PULSE-NCCL
evidence.baseline: ByteCheckpoint-NCCL; PULSE-NCCL (direct NCCL and disk-mediated variants)
evidence.condition: Qwen3-8B, 8 H200 GPUs, same high-bandwidth cluster, AReaL-DTE direct sparse point-to-point path
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 12 (Table 3, Section 5.4); PDF Page 13 (Conclusion)

evidence.claim: Transferred data volume: on Qwen3-30B-A3B AReaL-DTE produces Zstd-compressed sparse files of only 2.53-2.87 GB vs ~44.5 GB for ByteCheckpoint's compressed dense files (16.3x smaller on average), even though <2% of weights change, because every sparse entry stores both an int32 index and a BF16 value. On Qwen3-8B, AReaL-DTE reduces average Zstd-compressed artifact size by 19.7x relative to ByteCheckpoint.
evidence.value: Qwen3-30B-A3B sparse 2.53-2.87 GB vs dense ~44.5 GB (16.3x smaller); Qwen3-8B 19.7x smaller vs ByteCheckpoint; <2% weights change
evidence.condition: Zstd compression, <2% BF16 weight elements change between consecutive policy versions
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 12 (Section 5.3, Figure 3a-b)

evidence.claim: Peak memory (Table 2b, Qwen3-30B-A3B cross-cluster): AReaL-DTE GPU 71.52-71.96 GB / CPU 37.44-40.75 GB vs ByteCheckpoint GPU ~121 GB / CPU ~121-125 GB and PULSE GPU ~128-129 GB / CPU ~138-140 GB. AReaL-DTE reduces peak GPU memory by at least 40% and peak CPU memory by at least 66% relative to storage-mediated baselines (abstract reports ~41% GPU / >=87% CPU in same-cluster Qwen3-30B-A3B). Same-cluster Qwen3-8B peak CPU memory 3.45-3.48 GB vs 34.08-34.16 GB (ByteCheckpoint-NCCL) and 36.09-36.53 GB (PULSE-NCCL).
evidence.value: Qwen3-30B-A3B GPU ~71 GB vs ~121/~128 GB; CPU ~37-40 GB vs ~121-125/~138-140 GB; >=40% GPU, >=66% CPU reduction (cross-cluster); same-cluster Qwen3-8B CPU 3.45-3.48 GB
evidence.condition: Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3-8B, H200 GPUs, peak memory during construction/staging/communication/application
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 11 (Table 2b); PDF Page 12 (Section 5.3, 5.4); PDF Page 13 (same-cluster Qwen3-8B CPU)

evidence.claim: Training-loop overhead (Figure 4, normalized as T_weight_sync / T_step_without_weight): at 10 Gbps AReaL-DTE overhead is 0.68-0.99x the policy-training time across the four workloads (Qwen3-30B-A3B 0.92-0.99x; Qwen3-8B 0.68-0.99x), whereas ByteCheckpoint and PULSE still incur 5.75-6.56x and 2.14-2.37x respectively. AReaL-DTE reduces weight synchronization from a dominant bottleneck to a cost comparable to or lower than the remaining training step.
evidence.value: at 10 Gbps AReaL-DTE 0.68-0.99x training time vs ByteCheckpoint 5.75-6.56x and PULSE 2.14-2.37x
evidence.condition: cross-cluster, 10 Gbps, normalized to training-step time excluding weight sync
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 10 (Figure 4); PDF Page 12-13 (Section 5.4, Conclusion)

facts.evaluation_context: Hardware: NVIDIA H200 GPUs; Qwen3-8B uses 8 GPUs, Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE) uses 16 GPUs. Models span dense (Qwen3-8B) and mixture-of-experts (Qwen3-30B-A3B) architectures. Workloads: four online RL datasets (GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH-500, LogiQA). Deployment: same-cluster (one high-bandwidth cluster, AReaL-DTE direct sparse point-to-point; baselines use direct NCCL and disk-mediated variants) and cross-cluster (training and rollout workers do not share an NCCL group; all methods use storage-mediated paths via Alibaba Cloud OSS with Zstd compression; effective inter-cluster bandwidths 0.1/1/10 Gbps). Cross-cluster latency is DERIVED as T_same,disk + T_upload,p50(B) + T_download,p50(B) (median storage-transfer times), not a direct end-to-end measurement. Baselines: ByteCheckpoint (dense complete-state checkpoint, parallelism-independent representation, load-time remapping) and PULSE (transfers changed BF16 values but retains previous checkpoint). Metrics: E2E synchronization latency (construction+communication+application for same-cluster; derived for cross-cluster) and peak GPU/CPU memory during construction/staging/communication/application.
facts.limitations: The cross-cluster E2E latency is a DERIVED metric (T_same,disk + median upload + median download over OSS), not a direct end-to-end measurement of a real cross-cluster run; p50 storage-transfer times hide tail behavior and OSS-specific dynamics. Only two baselines (ByteCheckpoint, PULSE) are compared; other relevant systems (TensorHub reference-oriented transfer, ROSE shard/sparsity-aware transfer, DORA multi-version, Laminar relay workers, Weave) are discussed as related work but not benchmarked. RL correctness/staleness impact is out of scope: AReaL-DTE optimizes the data-plane synchronization operation, not the rollout schedule, RL algorithm, or consistency policy, so any effect of sparse/asynchronous publication on training convergence is not measured here. Evaluation is limited to two Qwen3 models and four math/code/QA RL datasets; other model families and non-RL workloads are not covered. The <2% changed-weight fraction is workload-dependent and may not hold for other RL algorithms or training regimes. Absolute synchronization latency at 10 Gbps still equals 0.68-0.99x of the training step, so weight sync remains a non-trivial fraction of the loop even with AReaL-DTE.
facts.project_relevance: Relevant to the cross-region card's question of how compression, incremental/delta transfer, and placement reduce bandwidth and latency for moving large model/cache state across clusters: AReaL-DTE is a concrete snapshot-free delta-transfer engine that exploits <2% per-step weight sparsity to cut transferred volume 16.3x-19.7x (Zstd-compressed sparse vs dense) and cut cross-cluster sync latency up to 19.9x (vs ByteCheckpoint) / 3.2x (vs PULSE) at 10 Gbps, reducing weight-sync overhead to <=the training-step time. The on-demand AdamW-inversion reconstruction (avoiding a persistent historical snapshot) and receiver-local coordinate remapping are concrete instances of the card's 'incremental transfer + placement' levers for bridging heterogeneous layouts. Caveat for project use: the cross-cluster number is a derived metric over OSS, not a direct WAN measurement, and the workload is policy-weight sync for RL post-training rather than KV-cache or agent-cache transfer; nonetheless it is a directly relevant technique for making frequent cross-cluster state publication cheap.

facts.title: Scaling Agentic AI Factories Through Extreme Co-Design with NVIDIA BlueField
facts.event_hint: NVIDIA BlueField-4 / Vera BlueField-4 STX + DOCA platform positioning for agentic AI factory data-path offload (context-memory via DOCA Memos).
facts.problem: Agentic inference extends beyond model execution into a distributed workflow of tool calls, retrieval, KV-cache persistence, policy checks, storage and network transfers; infrastructure services running on host CPUs contend with agent execution inside the reasoning loop and can stall tool execution, retrieval and validation even when GPU compute is available, while GPU memory pressure forces KV-cache eviction, recompute or context-length limits that trade latency, throughput and cost.
facts.mechanism: BlueField-4 DPU (up to 800 Gb/s Ethernet/InfiniBand, 64-core Grace CPU, LPDDR5X, PCIe Gen6) and the Vera BlueField-4 STX Storage Processor (Vera CPU + ConnectX-9 + up to 1.6 Tb/s Spectrum-X) run networking, storage, security, telemetry and control-plane services in a dedicated in-silicon domain outside the host. DOCA exposes these as programmable services: DOCA HBN (server-side L3/BGP on BlueField), BlueField ASTRA (Spectrum-X zero-trust multi-tenant bare-metal control point with ConnectX-9), DOCA Memos (cross-node KV-cache management/sharing), and DOCA security services (zero-trust access, policy, runtime visibility, isolation). The STX storage processor runs KV I/O, KV-metadata tracking, queue management, cache recall/pre-staging and tenant policy close to the storage/network path instead of presenting flash as block storage, powering the NVIDIA CMX context-memory tier between GPU memory and shared storage.

evidence.claim: BlueField-4 integrates up to 800 Gb/s Ethernet or InfiniBand, a 64-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, high-bandwidth LPDDR5X memory, PCIe Gen6, inline acceleration and the DOCA software platform.
evidence.value: up to 800 Gb/s; 64-core Grace CPU; PCIe Gen6; LPDDR5X
evidence.condition: BlueField-4 DPU specifications, Vera Rubin platform
evidence.source_locator: Section: BlueField powers the operating system of the AI factory

evidence.claim: Compared with BlueField-3, BlueField-4 doubles networking bandwidth, delivers up to 6x more compute performance, 4x memory capacity and more than 3x memory bandwidth.
evidence.value: 2x networking bandwidth; up to 6x compute; 4x memory capacity; >3x memory bandwidth
evidence.condition: BlueField-4 vs BlueField-3 (architectural comparison, no workload defined)
evidence.source_locator: Section: BlueField powers the operating system of the AI factory

evidence.claim: The Vera BlueField-4 STX Storage Processor combines the NVIDIA Vera CPU, ConnectX-9 SuperNIC, up to 1.6 Tb/s Spectrum-X Ethernet, NVMe storage access, accelerated data movement, in-silicon security and DOCA programmability.
evidence.value: up to 1.6 Tb/s Spectrum-X; ConnectX-9; Vera CPU
evidence.condition: STX storage processor specifications
evidence.source_locator: Section: BlueField powers the operating system of the AI factory

evidence.claim: DOCA Memos manages and shares KV cache across compute and storage nodes so context can be reused across long-context and agentic inference; KV-cache reuse reduces repeated prefill, context recomputation, GPU idle time and unnecessary data movement.
evidence.value: KV-cache reuse across compute and CMX data nodes
evidence.baseline: recompute/eviction of KV cache on GPU memory pressure
evidence.condition: long-context and agentic workloads via DOCA Memos + NVIDIA CMX context-memory tier
evidence.source_locator: Section: System-level capabilities of BlueField; Section: AI-native storage and context memory

evidence.claim: BlueField-4 operates as the infrastructure processor in the GPU compute tray for frontend (north-south) networking, host CPU offload, secure data access, management, observability and isolation, with higher frontend bandwidth and lower host CPU contention claimed to support more predictable inference latency and higher tokens per second per user.
evidence.value: more predictable inference latency; higher tokens per second per user (directional, no magnitude)
evidence.condition: directional benefit stated without a quantified benchmark
evidence.source_locator: Section: GPU compute: Securing and accelerating Rubin GPUs

facts.evaluation_context: NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform co-design: Rubin GPUs, Vera CPUs, NVLink scale-up, ConnectX-9 + Spectrum-X scale-out, BlueField-4 DPU, Vera BlueField-4 STX storage processor, NVIDIA CMX context-memory tier, DOCA software. Target workload is agentic AI factories (multi-turn agents, long-context reasoning, RAG, multi-agent). The evidence is architectural/positioning prose; no benchmark table, hardware configuration, measured latency/throughput/CPU-utilization numbers, or baseline workload are disclosed in the visible Evidence Pack.
facts.limitations: This is a vendor technical blog, not a measurement paper. The Evidence Pack exposes only architectural claims and directional benefits (higher GPU utilization, more predictable latency, lower cost per token, more tokens per watt, 2x/6x/4x/3x vs BlueField-3) with no workload-defined benchmark, no measured CPU-offload percentage, no end-to-end latency or throughput figures, and no deployment scale. The 6x/4x/3x comparisons are silicon-spec ratios versus BlueField-3, not agentic-workload results. Quantitative validation of KV-cache-reuse gain (tokens per second, power efficiency) is asserted but not measured in the visible text.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to the DPU inline-offload topic: BlueField-4 + DOCA Memos is a concrete instance of moving KV-cache management, storage metadata, security, telemetry and control-plane services into the DPU/storage-processor in-path domain rather than the host CPU, which is the project's core question of which data-path operations can run inline on a DPU and whether single-point offload can form an end-to-end gain. The CMX + DOCA Memos path is the most project-relevant抓手 for cross-domain KV-cache/context-memory offload; the next verification step is finding any measured CPU-offload, latency or tokens-per-second/watt numbers for agentic workloads under this stack.

evidence_gaps.question: Are there measured quantitative results for agentic workloads (CPU-offload percentage, end-to-end latency, tokens per second, tokens per watt, KV-cache reuse hit rate) on the BlueField-4 + DOCA Memos stack?
What is the concrete deployment scale or configuration for the claimed BlueField-4 gains inside a Vera Rubin AI factory?

facts.title: PTStore (Prefix Tensor Store): Distributed Prefix Caching and Replication for High Throughput Inference Serving
facts.event_hint: PTStore: a distributed prefix caching and replication system that stores reusable KV-cache prefix tensors across nodes/GPUs to accelerate LLM inference, from JHU and Argonne.
facts.problem: Existing inference runtimes (vLLM, DeepSpeed-MII, LMCache, Mooncake, SGLang) cache KV results mostly in local GPU/host memory; they lack support for aggregating distributed memory tiers, so cross-node prefix reuse requires regenerating the KV cache, causing load imbalance when popular tensors concentrate on a few servers and capping total KV-cache capacity.
facts.mechanism: Inspired by CDN client-caching, PTStore distributes and replicates popular tensors that form reusable KV-cache prefixes across distributed nodes and GPUs. It uses incremental tensor storage to minimize redundancy, consolidated metadata for rapid longest-common-prefix (LCP) queries, and a replication strategy optimizing local access to hot prefixes. Clients issue LCP queries (broadcast+reduce) and read/write tensor subsets via optimized RDMA built on the Mochi composable stack (Thallium C++ wrapper over Mercury and Argobots), progressing multiple servers in parallel. It integrates with existing LLM runtimes (e.g., vLLM).

evidence.claim: PTStore executes inferences on long-passage Q&A datasets 5-6 times more efficiently than current baselines that do not aggregate memory across nodes/GPUs and therefore regenerate the KV cache.
evidence.baseline: baselines that do not aggregate memory across nodes/GPUs (require KV cache regeneration)
evidence.condition: long-passage Q&A datasets (abstract claim)
evidence.source_locator: Evidence locator: PDF Page 1 - Abstract

evidence.claim: In TTFT scalability tests (1k-8k tokens, vLLM, SQUAD), PTStore outperforms vLLM's prefix caching starting at 2k tokens and is almost 2x faster at 8k tokens.
evidence.value: ~2x faster
evidence.condition: vLLM runtime, SQUAD dataset, 8k token sequences, TTFT metric
evidence.source_locator: Evidence locator: PDF Page 12 - Fig.4a

evidence.claim: PTStore is more than 2x faster than EvoStore for 1k-token sequences and about 20% faster for 8k tokens, with the advantage attributed to prefix replication (Fig.4b I/O vs compute breakdown).
evidence.condition: TTFT, SQUAD dataset, 1k and 8k token sequences
evidence.source_locator: Evidence locator: PDF Page 12

evidence.claim: Experimental evaluations show PTStore significantly reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) versus state of the art by up to an order of magnitude and remains scalable across variable sequence lengths.
evidence.value: up to an order of magnitude
evidence.condition: TTFT metric, scaling experiments
evidence.source_locator: Evidence locator: PDF Page 12 - 7 Conclusions

evidence.claim: Workloads use WikiQA (3,000 questions, page lengths 2,000-40,000 tokens) for scaling experiments and SQUAD (100,000 questions) for reading-comprehension extractive tasks; both are long-prompt/short-answer workloads that stress the prefill stage.
evidence.value: WikiQA 3,000 Q / SQUAD 100,000 Q
evidence.condition: extractive long-context Q&A workloads
evidence.source_locator: Evidence locator: PDF Page 9 - Workloads

facts.evaluation_context: Research prototype (JHU + Argonne) evaluated on extractive long-context Q&A (WikiQA, SQUAD). Communication uses optimized bulk RDMA via Mochi/Thallium. Reported metrics focus on TTFT and end-to-end runtime; sequence lengths tested 1k-8k tokens. No TPOT, token throughput, network utilization, or end-to-end P95 latency numbers are visible in the Evidence Pack; no production hardware spec or deployment scale (node/GPU counts) is exposed.
facts.limitations: TTFT and end-to-end runtime are the main reported metrics; decode-phase (TPOT), token throughput, and P95 latency are not reported in the visible evidence. Hardware platform, exact node/GPU counts, and RDMA fabric specs are not exposed. Results are specific to extractive long-context Q&A workloads (long prompt, short answer) which favor prefill optimization; performance on short prompts or decode-heavy chat workloads is not characterized. For small query lengths vLLM's baseline prefix caching is superior, per the authors.
facts.project_relevance: PTStore is a distributed prefix-cache storage layer using RDMA for cross-node KV-cache access, directly relevant to KVCache-aware network/bandwidth scheduling and the TPN question of whether network-side mechanisms reduce cross-node KVCache transfer and improve TTFT. It offers a concrete reference point for how distributed KV-cache aggregation changes the storage/network boundary, though it is a research prototype, not an Alibaba TPN product.
source_notes: arXiv preprint 2607.22648v1 (25 Jun 2026), FETCHED primary source.
Headline 5-6x efficiency gain is an abstract claim whose detailed baseline and workload condition are restated but the exact measurement table is in the unread suffix.
Comparison baselines are explicitly named: vLLM (prefix caching), EvoStore; related systems discussed include LMCache, Mooncake, SGLang (RadixAttention), Splitwise, DistServe.

facts.title: SK hynix Unveils First HBF Standard Specifications with SanDisk at FMS 2026
facts.event_hint: SK hynix and Sandisk published first open High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) standard specification via OCP at FMS 2026.
facts.problem: AI inference drives surging data volumes; existing memory hierarchy faces simultaneous bandwidth and capacity scalability bottlenecks that neither HBM nor SSDs alone resolve.
facts.mechanism: HBF is a new memory layer positioned between HBM and SSDs: it uses stacked NAND dies to deliver HBM-like high-speed transfer while significantly expanding capacity. The stack comes in 8-high and 16-high NAND die configurations; the host interconnect adopts the UCIe industry standard so HBF can attach to different processor types (GPUs, CPUs). The spec also defines connection interfaces/electrical characteristics, reliability and die-stack packaging guidelines, and software I/O guidelines.

evidence.claim: First HBF standard specification unveiled by SK hynix in collaboration with Sandisk via the Open Compute Project (OCP), positioned as an open industry standard.

facts.evaluation_context: Announcement-stage standard specification, not a measured product benchmark. No workload, hardware platform, latency, endurance (P/E), write-amplification, or power measurement is exposed in the visible evidence. Capacity (up to 512GB) and bandwidth (~0.4-3.0TB/s across Grade1-3) are specified ranges, not validated system results.
facts.limitations: Evidence is a vendor newsroom announcement of a specification, not independent characterization. No P/E endurance, access latency, write amplification, power draw, cost/bit, or volume-production timeline is visible. Headline summary claims of ~2.5x power-efficiency gain and ~540x capacity vs HBM are not supported by the visible Evidence Pack text and were not recorded as facts. Maturity (sampling vs mass production) is unspecified.
facts.project_relevance: HBF targets the AI inference bandwidth/capacity gap that influences storage-hierarchy and memory-attachment decisions. UCIe-based open standardization matters for processor-agnostic deployment, but the project card requires distinguishing announced specs from sampled or mass-production capability; here only an open specification and consortium status are confirmed.
source_notes: Source is an SK hynix newsroom announcement (vendor primary) loaded as LOCAL_SOURCE; numbers are specification targets, not measured benchmarks.
